# Exercise 1: Delineation of the Zwalm catchment {#sec-delineation}

from scripts.data_download.conf import XMIN, XMAX, YMIN, YMAX

## Assignment 

The delineation of a catchment based on a digital elevation model is often one of the first steps in a hydrological modelling study. The procedure is relatively straightforward, but the digital elevation model needs to be properly processed prior to the analysis. The pre-processing of the digital elevation model at least includes the removal of data gaps (i.e. spatial interpolation) and the removal of sinks (or depressions). Based on the processed DTM, the catchment can then be easily delineated using the simple principle that water always flows in the direction of the largest gradient. Different algorithms exist to do so (see course notes); here, only the gradient of every cell to its eight direct neighbours, the deterministic 8 (D8) algorithm, will be used.


::: {#tip-coordinates .callout-tip}
The outlet of the Zwalm catchment is located in the vicinity of $x$=101673 m and $y$=175377 m
:::

You can choose between 2 ways of performing this geospatial analysis:

- ![Python](figures/python-logo-only.png){height=1em} With [`pyflwdir`](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/), a pure Python package for flow direction data analysis, combined with [`rioxarray`](https://vylor.github.io/rioxarray/stable/), [`rasterio`](https://rasterio.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) and [`geopandas`](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/). A template is provided in `scripts/1_catchment_delineation.py`, to which you can add your own code. Each code cell in the template corresponds to one or more of the steps below. The [pyflwdir documentation](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/latest/) contains several examples which are useful as a starting point.
- ![QGIS](figures/qgis-icon.png){height=1em} With [QGIS](https://qgis.org/) as Graphical User Interface (GUI), using the [GRASS](https://grass.osgeo.org/) and [GDAL](https://gdal.org/en/stable/index.html) tools available via the Processing Toolbox. An overview of all GRASS functions can be found in the [tool manual](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass85/manuals/full_index.html).

::: {#wrn-dev-env .callout-warning collapse="true" title="Python option: installation requirements"}
The Python option requires packages that are **not** included in the environment in `environment.yml`. Install and activate the developer environment instead: `conda env create -f environment_dev.yml` and `conda activate hydromod_env_dev`.
:::

Specific tips for each choice of interface are denoted by their logo in the steps below.

1. Start by loading the DTM (see @sec-study-area-dtm), the river network from the *Vlaamse Hydrografische Atlas* and the catchment boundary from the *Oppervlaktewaterlichamen en hun afstroomgebieden, 2022-2027* dataset (see @sec-study-area-catchment-data). Check if the DTM is clipped to a reasonable region of interest around the Zwalm river (bounding box of approximately $x_{\mathrm{min}}=$ `{python} XMIN` m, $x_{\mathrm{max}}$ = `{python} XMAX` m, $y_{\mathrm{min}}$ = `{python} YMIN` m, $y_{\mathrm{max}}$ = `{python} YMAX` m).
    - ![Python](figures/python-logo-only.png){height=1em} Use [`rioxarray.open_rasterio`](https://vylor.github.io/rioxarray/stable/rioxarray.html#rioxarray-open-rasterio) for raster data and [`geopandas.read_file`](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/reference/api/geopandas.read_file.html#geopandas.read_file) for vector data.
2. Check if there are any missing values in the DTM. If so, spatially gap-fill it:
    - ![Python](figures/python-logo-only.png){height=1em} Compare the values with the nodata value. Missing values can be filled with [`rio.interpolate_na`](https://vylor.github.io/rioxarray/stable/rioxarray.html#rioxarray.raster_array.RasterArray.interpolate_na).
    - ![QGIS](figures/qgis-icon.png){height=1em} Use the `Fill nodata` tool (from GDAL).
3. Filter the digital elevation model for sinks (or depressions), fill them and calculate the flow direction of each grid cell using the D8 algorithm.
    - ![Python](figures/python-logo-only.png){height=1em} Use [`pyflwdir.from_dem`](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/latest/_generated/pyflwdir.from_dem.html), which fills the depressions and derives the D8 flow directions in a single step. The output of this function (here called `flw`) is a [FlwdirRaster](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/latest/_generated/pyflwdir.FlwdirRaster.html). The flow directions can be retrieved using the `to_array()` method (`flw.to_array()`). Check the [flow direction conventions](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/latest/_examples/flwdir.html#Flow-direction-data) to interpret the values.
    - ![QGIS](figures/qgis-icon.png){height=1em} Use [`r.fill.dir`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass85/manuals/r.fill.dir.html) to fill the sinks, followed by [`r.watershed`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass85/manuals/r.watershed.html) for the flow directions. Make sure that D8 is used as flow direction algorithm and that the minimum size of an exterior watershed basin is set to 500.
4. Calculate the flow accumulation (i.e. how many cells drain into each cell) and check if the accumulation map aligns with the actual river network of the Zwalm catchment.
    - ![Python](figures/python-logo-only.png){height=1em} Use [`upstream_area`](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/latest/_generated/pyflwdir.FlwdirRaster.upstream_area.html). 
    - ![QGIS](figures/qgis-icon.png){height=1em} The accumulation map is an output of `r.watershed` in the previous step.
5. Find the point with the largest accumulation on the Zwalm river. This point is the outlet of the catchment.
    - ![Python](figures/python-logo-only.png){height=1em} Select the Zwalm river from the river network and rasterise it to the same grid as the DTM using [`rasterio.features.rasterize`](https://rasterio.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/rasterio.features.html#rasterio.features.rasterize). Tip: use the [`xy`](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/latest/_generated/pyflwdir.FlwdirRaster.xy.html) method from pyflwdir to get the coordinates of raster index with the largest accumulation.
    - ![QGIS](figures/qgis-icon.png){height=1em} QGIS allows for a more visual inspection of the accumulation map. Rasterising the river network is therefore not strictly necessary and one can instead visually determine the point of largest accumulation near the Scheldt. If one would nonetheless want to rasterise the river network, use the `Rasterize (vector to raster)` tool (from GDAL).
6. Given the outlet determined in the previous step, delineate the catchment and vectorise the resulting raster map of the catchment.
    - ![Python](figures/python-logo-only.png){height=1em} Use [`basins`](https://deltares.github.io/pyflwdir/latest/_generated/pyflwdir.FlwdirRaster.basins.html) to delineate the catchment and supply the basin outlet to the function as parameter. Vectorise it with [`rasterio.features.shapes`](https://rasterio.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/rasterio.features.html#rasterio.features.shapes) and convert the result to a `GeoDataFrame` with [`geopandas.GeoDataFrame.from_features`](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/reference/api/geopandas.GeoDataFrame.from_features.html). 
    - ![QGIS](figures/qgis-icon.png){height=1em} Use [`r.water.outlet`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass85/manuals/r.water.outlet.html) to delineate the catchment and the `Polygonize (raster to vector)` tool (from GDAL) to vectorise it.
7. Repeat step 6 for the coordinates provided in @tip-coordinates. Compare the resulting catchment boundary with the one obtained in step 6 and with the provided catchment boundary from the *Oppervlaktewaterlichamen en hun afstroomgebieden, 2022-2027* dataset. What are the differences between these catchment boundaries? What could be the reasons for these differences?
8. Calculate the catchment area.

In your results and discussion below, make sure to include an overview figure of the Zwalm catchment including the DTM, river network and catchment boundary.
